collections.deduplication_policy: Papers remain evidence records, while recurring terminology and rhetorical moves are normalized into reusable entries and topic clusters.
collections.description: A manually audited, title-deduplicated set of 300 formally published papers for terminology, concept, and literature-navigation coverage.
collections.label: Recent five-year AI writing core
collections.selection_policy: Main-conference or formal journal papers only; select for field relevance and topic diversity, then manually remove title-level false positives.

abstracts_not_analyzed.reason: The DOI landing pages did not expose abstract text to the bounded HTML collector.

analysis_policy: Use official proceedings or conference HTML only.
Compute cross-document recurrence locally; do not retain or redistribute abstract text.
Manually reject proceedings boilerplate, repository links, decorative novelty claims, and near-duplicate formulations.
Promote only short collocations with at least two independent source attestations and an explicit usage boundary.

deduplication.policy: Recurring concepts map to shared topic and expression records; paper count does not determine expression count.

entries.avoid: Do not infer that every 3D-grounded VLA is a world model or that every world model predicts robot actions.
examples: Following {source}, we use '3D VLA world model' for a model that predicts {paper-specific outputs}.
Our system differs because it predicts {actions only or future observations only}.
entries.guidance: Attribute this formulation to the specific paper and describe its generated variables. Do not present the phrase as a universally standardized VLA architecture.
entries.meaning: In 3D-VLA, a model that uses 3D scene information and language-conditioned representations to generate future scene or action-related predictions for embodied manipulation.

provenance.note: Paper-specific terminology boundary independently paraphrased from 3D-VLA.

entries.avoid: Do not equate action chunking with open-loop execution; implementations may replan or aggregate overlapping chunks.
examples: The policy predicts a chunk of {k} future actions from the current observations.
We replan every {n} control steps and combine overlapping action chunks with {aggregation rule}.
entries.guidance: Report chunk length, execution or replanning frequency, overlap between chunks, and whether observations are incorporated again before the entire chunk is executed.
entries.meaning: Predicting a block of consecutive future actions in one policy inference step rather than predicting only the next action.

provenance.note: Independent definition based on action-chunk prediction in ACT and sequence prediction in visuomotor policies.

entries.avoid: Do not call ordinary data augmentation active perception.
examples: The task requires active perception because the agent must move to reveal {occluded or unobserved information}.
Actions affect both {task progress} and the observations available for future decisions.
entries.guidance: Describe the action-dependent sensing process and whether actions are chosen explicitly for information gain or jointly for task reward.
entries.meaning: Perception in which an agent's actions influence which observations become available, coupling information acquisition with control.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not call independent single-arm subtasks bimanual coordination unless their actions are coupled by the object or objective.
examples: The benchmark contains contact-rich bimanual tasks that require coordinated motion of both end effectors.
The policy jointly predicts left- and right-arm actions at {frequency} Hz.
entries.guidance: Specify whether coordination is symmetric or asymmetric, the control space for each arm, sensing, synchronization, and the task phase requiring coordination.
entries.meaning: Manipulation in which two robot arms or end effectors must act in a coordinated manner to accomplish a task.

provenance.note: Independent definition grounded in the bimanual manipulation setting studied by ACT.

entries.avoid: Do not claim cross-embodiment generalization when every evaluated robot appears in training under the same interface.
examples: We evaluate cross-embodiment transfer by adapting the pretrained policy to {held-out robot} with {amount of data}.
The embodiments differ in {morphology, camera setup, and action space}.
entries.guidance: State whether transfer is zero-shot, requires fine-tuning, or only shares pretraining. Reserve 'generalization' for a held-out evaluation that directly supports it.
entries.meaning: The application or adaptation of learned knowledge across robots or agents with different morphologies, sensors, action spaces, or control interfaces.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not equate a large aggregate trajectory count with balanced coverage across robots or tasks.
examples: We pretrain on a cross-robot mixture and fine-tune on demonstrations from the target embodiment.
The mixture sampling weights are chosen by {rule} rather than in proportion to raw dataset size.
entries.guidance: Report contributing datasets, sampling weights, action and observation normalization, license or availability constraints, and the target platforms used for evaluation.
entries.meaning: A training collection that combines trajectories from multiple robot platforms, embodiments, institutions, tasks, or data-generation pipelines.

provenance.note: Independent definition synthesized from Open X-Embodiment, Octo, and OpenVLA.

entries.avoid: Do not describe any stochastic policy as a diffusion policy.
examples: The diffusion policy generates an action sequence conditioned on {observation history}.
At inference, we execute {action horizon} actions from each denoised sequence before replanning.
entries.guidance: Specify the predicted horizon, conditioning observations, diffusion parameterization, sampling steps, and how generated actions are executed.
entries.meaning: A policy that represents a conditional distribution over actions or action sequences through a denoising diffusion process.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not use domain randomization as a generic label for ordinary image augmentation or claim coverage of the real domain without evaluation.
examples: During simulation training, we randomize {textures, lighting, camera, dynamics, or latency} over {specified ranges}.
Domain randomization exposes the policy to {variation} before real-world deployment.
entries.guidance: List randomized parameters and distributions, and separate visual randomization from dynamics randomization. Whether the real domain lies within effective support is an empirical question.
entries.meaning: Training over deliberately varied simulation parameters to make a model robust across a distribution intended to cover or bracket variability encountered in the real system.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not use 'embodied' for a passive model that only processes a fixed image or text dataset without an interaction formulation.
examples: We study embodied AI agents that perceive {sensory inputs} and act through {action space} in {environment}.
The agent's observations depend on its previous actions, creating a closed perception–action loop.
entries.guidance: Specify the body, sensors, action space, environment, and task. For simulated agents, state which physical or interaction constraints are modeled.
entries.meaning: The study of agents that perceive and act within an environment, where their observations, actions, and learning are shaped by embodiment and closed-loop interaction.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not assume that multimodal grounding alone makes the model a closed-loop robot controller.
examples: The embodied language model interleaves visual and state-estimation embeddings with text tokens.
The model supports {planning or question answering}, while a separate controller executes robot actions.
entries.guidance: Specify the sensor encoders, how their outputs enter the language model, the training tasks, and whether the system predicts language, plans, values, or executable actions.
entries.meaning: A language-model-based system that directly incorporates continuous or encoded sensor modalities to support reasoning or prediction grounded in an embodied environment.

provenance.note: Independent definition based on the embodied language-model formulation in PaLM-E.

entries.avoid: Do not call a policy generalist solely because one architecture is reused across several separately trained tasks.
examples: We train a generalist robot policy on {tasks, environments, and embodiments}.
We separately evaluate in-distribution multi-task performance and transfer to {new setting}.
entries.guidance: State the diversity actually represented in training and evaluation. Distinguish multi-task performance, zero-shot generalization, and fine-tuning ability.
entries.meaning: A policy trained across diverse tasks, environments, or robot data with the aim of supporting multiple behaviors and transfer beyond a single narrowly trained task.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not claim grounding when language is used only as an opaque class label.
examples: The agent grounds {instruction phrase} in {visual entities and state changes} before selecting actions.
We learn grounded instruction following from {demonstrations or interaction feedback}.
entries.guidance: State the grounding modalities and whether supervision includes demonstrations, symbolic plans, object annotations, or only task success.
entries.meaning: Mapping linguistic instructions to actions by relating language to perceived entities, spatial relations, state changes, and interaction possibilities in the environment.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not use multimodal to describe multiple views from the same modality without clarification.
examples: The agent fuses {vision} and {audio} to localize {target} from egocentric observations.
We align {language} with {visual and proprioceptive representations} before action prediction.
entries.guidance: Name the modalities and distinguish representation, alignment, fusion, translation, and co-learning. Explain which signals are available during training and deployment.
entries.meaning: Perception that integrates information from distinct sensory modalities, such as vision, audio, touch, language, or proprioception, for embodied decision making.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not call ordinary multimodal observations a task prompt unless they communicate the intended task or goal.
examples: The prompt interleaves a language instruction with images of the target objects.
We evaluate novel compositions of visual and textual prompt elements.
entries.guidance: List the modalities, tokenization, temporal order, and information available at test time. Distinguish a prompt that specifies a task from observations generated while executing it.
entries.meaning: A task specification composed of more than one modality, such as interleaved text, images, object crops, goals, or demonstrations.

provenance.note: Independent definition based on multimodal prompt specification in VIMA.

entries.avoid: Do not conflate ObjectNav with point-goal navigation, where the target is a coordinate.
examples: In ObjectNav, the agent receives {target category} and must navigate to a valid instance using {observations}.
entries.guidance: State target specification, sensors, environment split, success radius, stopping rule, and evaluation metrics such as success and path efficiency.
entries.meaning: An embodied navigation task in which an agent must reach an instance of a target object category from egocentric observations.

provenance.note: Benchmark-oriented task definition with protocol fields made explicit.

entries.avoid: Do not claim open-vocabulary generalization when test names are new strings for training-seen objects or skills.
examples: We evaluate open-vocabulary manipulation on held-out {objects, concepts, or instructions} while holding {other axis} fixed.
entries.guidance: Define the held-out unit, language source, object and task splits, perception assumptions, and any foundation-model supervision.
entries.meaning: Manipulation conditioned on object or task descriptions whose evaluation vocabulary is not restricted to a fixed closed set used during task-specific training.

provenance.note: Operational definition centered on the held-out vocabulary axis.

entries.avoid: Do not call ordinary recurrent inference adaptation unless the changing context and adaptation mechanism are made explicit.
examples: The adaptation module infers {environment context} from a recent history of {states and actions}.
The base policy responds to changing {terrain or dynamics} without gradient updates at deployment.
entries.guidance: Specify what adapts, whether policy parameters change, the adaptation window, supervision, and latency.
entries.meaning: Updating an internal estimate, context, or behavior during deployment from a short history of recent interaction so the policy can respond to changing dynamics or conditions.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not claim zero-shot sim-to-real if any real-world fine-tuning or calibration materially updates the policy.
examples: We evaluate zero-shot sim-to-real transfer by deploying the simulation-trained policy without {real-world policy updates}.
The transfer gap arises from mismatches in {appearance, dynamics, sensing, or actuation}.
entries.guidance: Name what transfers, what is randomized or adapted, the real-world evaluation, and whether real data is used before deployment.
entries.meaning: Training or developing a model in simulation and deploying or adapting it to a physical system whose observations or dynamics differ from the simulator.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not call a pipeline visuomotor if vision only labels a dataset and is unavailable to the deployed controller.
examples: The visuomotor policy maps {image history and proprioception} to {action chunk}.
We train the policy end to end from {visual input} to {robot command}.
entries.guidance: Specify visual inputs, auxiliary conditioning, action representation, control frequency, and whether perception and control are trained end to end.
entries.meaning: A policy that maps visual observations, often together with proprioception or goals, to motor actions or action sequences.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not call a vision-language model a VLA merely because its textual output can be interpreted by an external planner.
examples: The VLA policy maps camera observations and a language instruction to a sequence of robot actions.
We fine-tune the pretrained VLA on {number} demonstrations from {target embodiment}.
entries.guidance: Specify all inputs, the action space, control frequency, training data, and whether actions are generated directly, discretized as tokens, or decoded by a separate head.
entries.meaning: A model or policy that conditions on visual observations and language and produces robot actions or an action representation for embodied control.

provenance.note: Independent definition synthesized across open, cross-embodiment, and 3D VLA papers.

entries.avoid: Do not conflate VLN with object-goal navigation that has no free-form instruction.
examples: In VLN, the agent maps a route instruction and a sequence of egocentric observations to navigation actions.
We evaluate generalization to {unseen environments or instructions}.
entries.guidance: Specify environment type, action space, instruction source, navigation graph or continuous control, and generalization split.
entries.meaning: A task in which an embodied agent follows a natural-language route instruction by grounding it in visual observations and selecting navigation actions.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not treat 2D versus 3D representation as the only meaningful difference when memory and interaction regimes also differ.
examples: Embodied approaches vary in their geometric representation ({geometry}), temporal memory ({memory}), interaction regime ({regime}), and supervision ({signals}).
entries.expression: Embodied systems should be grouped by geometry, memory, interaction, and supervision.
entries.guidance: Use only axes that materially separate the cited methods and verify every assigned category.
entries.meaning: A Related Work scaffold that distinguishes representational and data assumptions instead of listing agents by publication date.

provenance.note: Original literature-synthesis scaffold, not a source-derived sentence.

entries.avoid: Do not group methods only by architecture when their data and deployment assumptions dominate the comparison.
examples: We organize prior work by its supervision signal, whether training uses online interaction, and the sensory information available at deployment.
Unlike methods trained on {data regime}, our approach assumes {different verified regime}.
entries.expression: Embodied methods should be positioned by supervision, interaction regime, and deployment assumptions.
entries.guidance: Use concrete axes such as demonstrations versus rewards, simulation versus real data, online versus offline collection, and privileged versus deployable observations.
entries.meaning: Structures embodied-AI related work around how data is obtained, whether learning is interactive, and what information or hardware is available at deployment.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; example wording is original.

entries.avoid: Do not use the term for a single-frame 3D feature tensor that is not maintained across interaction.
examples: The agent updates a 3D scene memory with {features} in {coordinate frame} and queries it for {task}.
entries.guidance: Specify coordinate frame, stored features, update rule, memory lifetime, and how queries access the memory.
entries.meaning: A persistent spatial representation that aggregates observations into a three-dimensional memory for embodied exploration, grounding, or reasoning.

provenance.note: Canonicalized representation term from recent embodied 3D systems.

entries.avoid: Do not assume that language-token and action-token probabilities have the same semantics or that tokenization is lossless.
examples: Each action dimension is discretized into {number} bins and represented by a dedicated token range.
The predicted action tokens are decoded into {control command} at {frequency} Hz.
entries.guidance: Describe discretization bins, dimensions, control semantics, decoding, clipping, and any embodiment-specific normalization.
entries.meaning: A representation that maps continuous or structured robot controls into discrete tokens or token-like outputs for sequence-model prediction.

provenance.note: Technical terminology indexed from RT-X and OpenVLA action-generation formulations.

entries.avoid: Do not call semantic relevance an affordance unless it expresses an action possibility or interaction relation.
examples: The model grounds {instruction or action} to {object, region, or pose} that affords {interaction}.
entries.guidance: Name the affordance representation, grounding target, supervision source, and whether feasibility is verified by execution.
entries.meaning: The association of a task or action description with scene regions, objects, poses, or interactions that support the action.

provenance.note: Cross-topic term with semantic and execution boundaries.

entries.avoid: Do not describe a third-person camera or global map as egocentric.
examples: At each step, the agent receives an egocentric {RGB, depth, or audio-visual} observation.
The policy does not access {global map or privileged state}.
entries.guidance: Name the modality and field of view, and distinguish current observations from accumulated maps or privileged simulator state.
entries.meaning: Sensory input represented from the agent's current first-person viewpoint rather than from a fixed external or global viewpoint.

provenance.note: Canonical term indexed from linked primary papers; examples are original.

entries.avoid: Do not use embodiment as a synonym for environment or task.
examples: The policy is evaluated on embodiments that differ in {morphology, sensors, or action space}.
We encode embodiment-specific {proprioceptive or action information}.
entries.guidance: Name the aspects that differ across embodiments—camera placement, morphology, control frequency, action coordinates, or dynamics—rather than using the term abstractly.
entries.meaning: The agent-specific physical or simulated form that determines its sensing, actuation, kinematics, and interaction constraints.

provenance.note: Canonical term indexed from linked primary papers; examples are original.

entries.avoid: Do not call an image-plane grasp rectangle a full 6-DoF grasp pose.
examples: The network predicts 6-DoF grasp poses from {RGB-D image or point cloud}.
We transform each grasp pose from {camera frame} to {robot base frame}.
entries.guidance: Define the coordinate frame, gripper model, collision checks, and evaluation criterion. Separate pose proposal quality from executed grasp success.
entries.meaning: A candidate gripper pose in three-dimensional space parameterized by three translational and three rotational degrees of freedom.

provenance.note: Canonical term indexed from linked primary papers; examples are original.

entries.avoid: Do not use the term for synthetic variation or a single staged room.
examples: The dataset contains in-the-wild robot data collected across {sites, scenes, and tasks}.
We evaluate whether collection diversity improves robustness to {held-out environment variation}.
entries.guidance: Quantify collectors, sites, scenes, robots, tasks, and collection protocol. 'In the wild' describes collection diversity, not unrestricted deployment.
entries.meaning: Robot interaction data collected across naturally varied real-world scenes, tasks, operators, or institutions rather than within one tightly controlled laboratory setup.

provenance.note: Canonical term indexed from linked primary papers; examples are original.

entries.avoid: Do not imply compositional language understanding unless it is evaluated under an appropriate held-out split.
examples: The language-conditioned policy predicts actions from {camera views}, proprioception, and the instruction.
We evaluate whether the policy follows unseen combinations of familiar language concepts.
entries.guidance: State the language granularity, observation modalities, action horizon, and whether language changes the task, goal, or low-level behavior.
entries.meaning: A control policy whose action prediction depends jointly on sensory observations and a linguistic task specification or instruction.

provenance.note: Field-standard terminology indexed from generalist robot-policy and multimodal-prompt work.

entries.avoid: Do not call a task long-horizon solely because episodes have a large maximum length.
examples: The task requires long-horizon interaction across {number} dependent subgoals.
Early execution errors can alter the states available to later subgoals.
entries.guidance: Quantify horizon in steps, subgoals, elapsed time, or state changes, and explain what makes dependencies consequential.
entries.meaning: A task requiring a temporally extended sequence of dependent decisions, often with delayed outcomes and opportunities for errors to accumulate.

provenance.note: Canonical term indexed from linked primary papers; examples are original.

entries.avoid: Do not use multimodal to mean that the input has multiple sensor modalities.
examples: The policy must represent a multimodal action distribution because {multiple strategies} are valid for the same observation.
We visualize samples corresponding to {distinct action modes}.
entries.guidance: Explain the source of multimodality and evaluate mode coverage or task success; multiple samples do not by themselves establish meaningful modes.
entries.meaning: An action distribution with multiple distinct high-probability behaviors, such as different valid trajectories for accomplishing the same task.

provenance.note: Canonical term indexed from linked primary papers; examples are original.

entries.avoid: Do not treat pushing as a failed grasp; it can be an intentional non-prehensile action.
examples: The policy coordinates prehensile grasping with non-prehensile pushing to {task objective}.
Pushing changes the scene configuration before a grasp is attempted.
entries.guidance: Use the distinction to describe action primitives or coordination between them. Name the actual contact modes studied.
entries.meaning: Prehensile manipulation secures an object with a grasp, whereas non-prehensile manipulation changes object state through actions such as pushing without maintaining a grasp.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not include external camera observations under proprioception.
examples: The policy conditions on visual features and proprioceptive observations comprising {signals}.
We synchronize proprioception with {camera frames} at {rate}.
entries.guidance: List the included signals, normalization, sampling rate, and temporal alignment with exteroceptive observations.
entries.meaning: Internal measurements of the agent's body state, such as joint positions, velocities, actuator states, or inertial readings.

provenance.note: Canonical term indexed from linked primary papers; examples are original.

entries.avoid: Do not attribute every real-world failure to the reality gap without diagnosis.
examples: We study the visual component of the reality gap while holding {controller or dynamics} fixed.
Residual failures are associated with mismatches in {specific factor}.
entries.guidance: Identify the relevant mismatch instead of treating the gap as a single scalar phenomenon.
entries.meaning: The discrepancy between simulated and physical observations, dynamics, contacts, sensors, or actuation that can degrade real-world deployment.

provenance.note: Canonical term indexed from linked primary papers; examples are original.

entries.avoid: Do not treat 'task-agnostic' as a universally standardized term or imply absence of task conditioning merely because parameters are shared.
examples: The model uses joint multi-task training with shared parameters and conditions on {task instruction}.
Following {source}, we use 'task-agnostic training' to mean {paper-specific definition}.
entries.guidance: Prefer the more explicit phrase 'joint multi-task training with shared parameters' unless discussing the cited paper's terminology. Explain what task information remains available, such as language commands.
entries.meaning: In RT-1, this label describes joint training with shared parameters across a broad task collection rather than separate task-specific models.

provenance.note: Paper-specific term indexed from the linked primary source; examples are original.

entries.avoid: Do not compare success rates computed with different horizons, reset policies, human interventions, or success detectors without qualification.
examples: Task success rate is computed over {number} independent trials using {completion criterion}.
The policy succeeds in {count}/{total} trials, corresponding to {percentage}%.
entries.guidance: Define the success criterion, trial unit, number of trials, aggregation level, and treatment of partial completion and timeouts. Provide uncertainty where appropriate.
entries.meaning: The fraction or percentage of evaluation trials that satisfy a predefined task-completion criterion.

provenance.note: Field-standard evaluation terminology indexed from manipulation and VLA papers.

entries.avoid: Do not use 'human demonstration' without distinguishing robot teleoperation from videos or state–action data generated outside the target robot.
examples: We collect {number} teleoperated demonstrations with a leader–follower interface.
The dataset retains both successful and unsuccessful teleoperation episodes.
entries.guidance: Report the interface, observation available to the operator, control rate, filtering, intervention policy, and whether unsuccessful attempts are retained.
entries.meaning: A robot trajectory collected while a human operator controls the robot through a physical, graphical, wearable, or other remote interface.

provenance.note: Field-standard data-collection terminology indexed from ALOHA and DROID.

entries.avoid: Do not confuse temporal ensembling with an ensemble of independently trained policies.
examples: At each control step, we aggregate overlapping action predictions using exponentially decaying weights.
Temporal ensembling smooths predictions from successive action chunks.
entries.expression: temporal ensembling of overlapping action predictions
entries.guidance: Describe the weighting function, overlap window, and whether aggregation occurs in action space or another representation. Mark ACT-specific weighting choices as implementation details rather than universal definitions.
entries.meaning: Combining action predictions made at different policy-query times for the same future control step.

provenance.note: Method terminology indexed from ACT and generalized only at the level of overlapping action predictions.

entries.avoid: Do not infer the control-feedback structure solely from the number of actions output by the network.
examples: Although the policy predicts {k} actions, it replans after executing {n}, using a new observation.
The controller executes the entire chunk open-loop before the next policy query.
entries.expression: separate prediction horizon, execution horizon, and feedback frequency
entries.guidance: Report all three quantities and explain how overlapping predictions are combined. Use 'closed-loop' only when updated observations influence subsequent executed actions.
entries.meaning: A policy may predict many future actions while executing only part of them before receiving a new observation, so action horizon alone does not determine whether control is open-loop or closed-loop.

provenance.note: Independent reporting guidance synthesized from chunked and diffusion-based action policies.

entries.avoid: Do not use embodiment gap as an unexplained catch-all for every domain shift.
examples: We isolate physical disparity in {factor} from visual disparity in {factor} and evaluate each under {controlled protocol}.
entries.expression: decompose the embodiment gap into physical and visual disparities
entries.guidance: Evaluate or discuss physical and visual shifts separately before attributing transfer failure to embodiment as a single factor.
entries.meaning: Differences between training and deployment embodiments can arise from morphology and dynamics as well as camera geometry, appearance, sensing, and observation statistics.

provenance.note: Factorized reporting guidance grounded in recent embodiment-transfer studies.

entries.avoid: Do not describe actions as standardized when only file formats are shared but control semantics remain different.
examples: We map each dataset's controls into a common {representation} and retain an embodiment-specific action mask.
Actions are normalized per embodiment before joint training and decoded with {adapter}.
entries.expression: heterogeneous robot action spaces require an explicit alignment strategy
entries.guidance: Specify coordinate frames, normalization, missing dimensions, embodiment identifiers, and decoding into each robot's native controller.
entries.meaning: Different datasets and embodiments may use controls with different dimensions, frames, grippers, rates, and semantics, so joint training requires a documented representation or adapter.

provenance.note: Independent implementation guidance synthesized from cross-embodiment policy and dataset work.

entries.avoid: Do not use the two terms as universally interchangeable when the algorithm is not direct supervised cloning.
examples: We use behavioral cloning to fit the policy to demonstration state–action pairs.
The method belongs to imitation learning but differs from behavioral cloning in {interactive or distributional mechanism}.
entries.guidance: Use behavioral cloning for the supervised objective and imitation learning for the wider family, which may include interactive data collection, occupancy matching, or other objectives.
entries.meaning: Imitation learning is the broader problem of learning behavior from demonstrations, while behavioral cloning usually denotes direct supervised prediction of expert actions from observations.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not collapse all held-out conditions into one generalization score that hides qualitatively different shifts.
examples: We report separate results for unseen objects, unseen task compositions, and unseen embodiments.
The hardest split holds out both {factor one} and {factor two} during training.
entries.expression: evaluate embodied generalization along separately controlled axes
entries.guidance: Define each split procedurally and report results by axis. Use 'zero-shot' only when the evaluated factor or combination was absent from training under the stated protocol.
entries.meaning: Systematic evaluation varies identified factors—such as objects, placements, task templates, prompt compositions, environments, or embodiments—while documenting which combinations were withheld.

provenance.note: Independent evaluation guidance synthesized from multimodal-prompt and cross-embodiment studies.

entries.avoid: Do not use VLA, vision-language model, and embodied language model interchangeably.
examples: Unlike embodied language models evaluated on reasoning tasks, our VLA directly predicts {robot control representation}.
The model supplies high-level plans to a separate low-level policy and is therefore not evaluated as an end-to-end VLA controller.
entries.expression: distinguish VLA policies from embodied language models
entries.guidance: Classify a method by its actual output and control interface rather than model backbone. Some systems may satisfy both descriptions, but the overlap should be stated.
entries.meaning: A VLA label emphasizes action generation for control, whereas an embodied language model may use sensor inputs for reasoning or prediction without directly producing executable actions.

provenance.note: Independent terminology boundary synthesized from PaLM-E and OpenVLA.

entries.avoid: Do not replace the phrase with an equally vague adjective such as 'strong generalizability.'
examples: We evaluate generalization to unseen {objects} and robustness to {perturbation}.
The policy succeeds under {specified shift} in {fraction} of trials.
entries.guidance: Prefer 'generalization to {held-out condition}', 'robustness to {perturbation}', or the exact measured outcome. 'Capability' is acceptable only when its scope is stated.
entries.meaning: These noun stacks often conceal the evaluated shift or perturbation and can sound like literal translations rather than operational claims.

provenance.note: Original anti-pattern guidance authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not intensify inherently comparative or absolute adjectives.
examples: {method} outperforms {baseline} on {metric} in {setting}.
entries.guidance: Use 'outperforms' for a verified metric comparison, 'is more effective' with a criterion, or simply report the numbers.
entries.meaning: Redundant comparative forms that obscure the actual comparison dimension.

provenance.note: Original anti-pattern guidance authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Avoid 'perform good', 'gets a good result', and comparison without a metric or baseline.
examples: {method} achieves higher {metric} than {baseline} under {protocol}.
entries.guidance: Use 'performs well' only for an informal summary; in papers, prefer 'achieves higher {metric}' or a quantified comparison.
entries.meaning: Non-idiomatic or underspecified performance wording often produced by literal translation.

provenance.note: Original anti-pattern guidance authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not use a direct comparison frame when data, compute, split, or evaluation protocol is materially incompatible without a caveat.
examples: We compare {method} to {baseline set} at a matched {data or interaction budget}.
entries.guidance: Name baselines and disclose protocol mismatches. 'Compare with' is also grammatical, but use one form consistently.
entries.meaning: Introduces a direct comparison set.

provenance.note: Short collocation independently attested in the linked primary papers; example is original.

entries.avoid: Do not use this phrase for an aspiration, untested mechanism, or causal conclusion unsupported by the experiment.
examples: We demonstrate that {method} {measured behavior} across {evaluated scope}.
entries.guidance: Use only for evidence actually reported in the paper, and bind the statement to its setting. Prefer 'show' or 'find' if 'demonstrate' would overstate the design.
entries.meaning: States a finding supported by the paper's experiments or analysis.

provenance.note: Short collocation independently attested in the linked primary papers; example is original.

entries.avoid: Do not use range to conceal a small or homogeneous evaluation set, and do not imply zero-shot transfer when adaptation is used.
examples: We assess {representation or model} on a range of downstream tasks under {adaptation protocol}: {named tasks}.
entries.guidance: Name the downstream tasks and state whether evaluation uses frozen features, prompting, fine-tuning, planning, or policy learning.
entries.meaning: Refers to several named applications used to test whether a learned representation, model, or policy transfers beyond its training objective.

provenance.note: Short recurring abstract collocation attested across three collection papers; example is original.

provenance.note: Short collocation independently attested in the linked primary papers; example is original.

provenance.note: Short collocation independently attested in the linked primary papers; example is original.

entries.expression: in both simulated and real-world {environments or experiments}

provenance.note: Short recurring abstract collocation attested across four collection papers; example is original.

provenance.note: Short recurring abstract collocation attested across three collection papers; example is original.

entries.expression: across a wide spectrum of {tasks or settings}

entries.meaning: Signals deliberately broad coverage across named tasks, settings, or conditions.

entries.meaning: Introduces a concrete research gap tied to a task and a named constraint.

entries.meaning: States the conceptual observation that motivates the method and connects it to a scoped capability.

provenance.note: Original section-aware pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

We develop {method}, a {method class} that {mechanism} for {task}.
entries.guidance: Replace the slots with the paper-level mechanism, not a list of low-level implementation details. Use the exact method name from the manuscript.
entries.meaning: Names the contribution and summarizes its operative mechanism and objective in one sentence.

provenance.note: Original section-aware pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Do not average incompatible tasks or select the largest favorable result while implying it summarizes the full study.
examples: Across {number} {tasks}, {method} improves {metric} by {value} percentage points over {comparator}.
Under {shift}, {method} reduces {error metric} from {baseline value} to {method value}.
entries.expression: Across {evaluation scope}, {method} changes {metric} by {value} relative to {comparator}.
entries.guidance: Specify whether the value is absolute, relative, or in percentage points. Use the same aggregation and comparison set as the referenced display.
entries.meaning: Reports one principal verified result with its evaluation scope, metric, magnitude, and comparator.

provenance.note: Original section-aware pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Avoid turning benchmark evidence into an unrestricted claim about real-world deployment or general intelligence.
examples: These results support {conclusion} for {task family} under {protocol}.
The evidence supports transfer across {held-out axis}, but does not establish {broader scope}.
entries.expression: These results support {scoped conclusion} under {evaluated conditions}.
entries.guidance: Name the datasets, tasks, shifts, assumptions, or system conditions that bound the conclusion when they are material.
entries.meaning: Closes an empirical summary with a conclusion bounded by the actual evaluation.

provenance.note: Original section-aware pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Do not mix rerun and copied numbers without labeling their provenance and compatibility.
examples: Baseline results are reproduced using the authors' {release} with {documented changes}.
Results marked with {symbol} are taken from {verified source}; all others are rerun under our protocol.
entries.expression: Baseline results are {rerun or sourced} using {implementation and version}.
entries.guidance: State code commit or release, consequential changes, tuning policy, and whether the reported protocol matches the present evaluation.
entries.meaning: Records whether baseline numbers were reproduced or taken from a source and identifies the implementation.

provenance.note: Original experimental-writing pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Do not claim a matched ablation when variants use different data, budgets, selection, or evaluation.

Component analysis on {task}; the full model is {row}, and each variant changes {factor}.
entries.expression: Ablation of {components} with all variants trained under {matched protocol}.
entries.guidance: Define component indicators, full-model row, metric, runs, uncertainty, and any retuning policy in the remaining caption.
entries.meaning: Introduces an ablation caption and states the matched condition needed to compare variants.

provenance.note: Original table-caption pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Do not label a table efficiency when it reports only parameter count or latency without task quality.
examples: Quality and deployment cost measured on {hardware} at {precision} and batch size {value}. Latency includes {boundary}.
Task success and control latency under {deployment protocol}; values report {statistic} over {repeats}.
entries.expression: Quality and deployment cost measured under {hardware and timing protocol}.
entries.guidance: Name hardware, precision, batch, input, warm-up, timing boundary, repeats, resource units, and metric directions.
entries.meaning: Frames an efficiency caption around both outcome quality and a reproducibly measured deployment resource.

provenance.note: Original table-caption pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Do not use 'unseen' without specifying what was withheld and whether it influenced model selection.
examples: Generalization from {training environments} to held-out {environments}. Test environments are excluded from training and validation.
Transfer from {embodiments} to unseen {embodiments}; success rates are averaged over {trials}.
entries.guidance: Continue with the held-out unit, selection protocol, metrics, runs, uncertainty, and reference condition.
entries.meaning: Names the training and held-out conditions at the start of a generalization-table caption.

provenance.note: Original table-caption pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Do not use a one-phrase caption that forces readers to reconstruct the protocol from the prose.
examples: Results on {tasks} under the {split} protocol. Higher {metric} is better; values are {units} and report {statistic} over {runs}.
Evaluation on {environment} with {budget}. Lower {metric} is better, and bold marks the best comparable result.
entries.expression: Results on {dataset or task} under {protocol}. {Metric direction and units}.
entries.guidance: Continue with aggregation, uncertainty, runs, emphasis, and protocol exceptions. Use the exact split and evaluation setting.
entries.meaning: Provides the first two functional sentences of a self-contained main-results caption.

provenance.note: Original table-caption pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Do not show only values near the chosen optimum or imply a scaling law from a narrow sweep.

Scaling with {data or model size}; bold identifies the configuration used for the main experiments, not an oracle test optimum.
entries.expression: Sensitivity to {parameter}; {default marker} denotes the selected configuration.
entries.guidance: State the full range, selection data and objective, fixed factors, runs, uncertainty, and changed resource when scale varies.
entries.meaning: Introduces a sensitivity caption and identifies the configuration used elsewhere in the paper.

provenance.note: Original table-caption pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Do not write 'the gains are due to' without an identifying intervention.
examples: These results are consistent with the hypothesis that {component or inductive bias} improves {measured behavior}.
entries.expression: These results are consistent with the hypothesis that {mechanism}.
entries.guidance: Use when evidence supports but does not isolate the proposed explanation. Follow with an ablation or limitation if available.
entries.meaning: Links observations to a mechanism without claiming that the experiment identifies causality.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not compare your full method with one isolated weakness of a baseline.
examples: Unlike {method family}, which relies on {assumption}, our approach {mechanism without that assumption}.
entries.expression: Unlike {comparison class}, which {defining behavior}, our approach {distinct behavior}.
entries.guidance: Keep the grammatical comparison parallel and verify that the characterization holds for the cited comparison class.
entries.meaning: Contrasts two methods on one explicit mechanism or assumption.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not use 'novel' as a substitute for explaining what is contributed.
examples: Our main contribution is {method or analysis} that {capability} under {evaluated conditions}.
entries.expression: Our main contribution is {artifact or insight} that {verified capability}.
entries.guidance: Name a method, analysis, dataset, benchmark, or finding. Bind the capability to the evaluated scope.
entries.meaning: States the central contribution and its demonstrated capability in one sentence.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not imply that a local convention is the field's only accepted definition.
examples: We use {term} to denote {entity or process satisfying explicit conditions}.
entries.guidance: Use when the paper needs a definition whose scope is specific to the present formulation. State the defining property, not a circular synonym.
entries.meaning: Introduces a local, operational meaning for a term.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not use this frame to silently redefine a standard term for rhetorical convenience.
examples: In this work, {term} refers specifically to {property within the studied setting}.
entries.expression: In this work, {term} refers to {scope-bounded definition}.
entries.guidance: Use when community usage is broader than the aspect studied in the paper. Follow with inclusions or exclusions if ambiguity remains.
entries.meaning: Defines a term while making the scope of the definition explicit.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

examples: We evaluate {method} on {benchmarks} using {metrics} under a matched {budget}.
We evaluate in {simulation or real system} on {tasks}, reporting {metrics} under {protocol}.
entries.guidance: Name the actual tasks, principal metrics, split or evaluation regime, and any material simulation or deployment condition.
entries.meaning: Introduces the evaluation scope, outcome measures, and protocol in one compact sentence.

provenance.note: Original experimental-writing pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

Among {denominator}, {fraction} involve {condition}; category labels were assigned using {procedure}.
entries.expression: Failure cases are dominated by {category}, accounting for {fraction} of {denominator}.
entries.guidance: Define a mutually interpretable failure taxonomy, label multi-cause cases, and state whether categories were assigned manually or automatically.
entries.meaning: Reports a failure category with its frequency and explicit denominator.

provenance.note: Original results-analysis pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.expression: For a controlled comparison, we hold {factor} fixed and vary only {factor}.
entries.guidance: Use only when the protocol truly controls the named factor; list remaining mismatches if they affect interpretation.
entries.meaning: Explains how an experiment isolates a comparison dimension.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not erase the contribution of the foundational method.

entries.expression: Our formulation builds on {foundation} and extends it to {new setting or capability}.
entries.guidance: Cite the foundation and explain what changes in the new formulation. Use 'extends' only when the technical relationship is real.
entries.meaning: States intellectual continuity and the precise extension contributed by the paper.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

examples: An important next step is to evaluate {capability} under {distribution shift or deployment condition}.
entries.expression: An important next step is to evaluate {capability} under {condition}.
entries.guidance: Use for work not completed in the current paper. Prefer a falsifiable next step over generic aspirations.
entries.meaning: Identifies a concrete unresolved evaluation or research direction.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.meaning: Identifies a research gap without dismissing prior progress.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.expression: The {split} holds out {unit} from all training and selection data.
entries.guidance: Name whether the unit is subject, scene, object, task, environment, embodiment, or temporal block. Disclose any preprocessing learned globally.
entries.meaning: Defines a held-out unit and excludes it from both model fitting and selection.

provenance.note: Original experimental-writing pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

Values are medians over {number} runs, with {interval} percentiles in parentheses.
entries.expression: We report {statistic} over {number} independent {runs or seeds}.
entries.guidance: Replace the statistical unit precisely and explain nested averaging when episodes or scenes occur within seeds. Name uncertainty separately.
entries.meaning: States the aggregation statistic and number of independent repetitions.

provenance.note: Original experimental-writing pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

Existing methods can be distinguished by {decision mechanism} and {interaction regime}.
entries.expression: Within {scope}, the closest approaches can be compared along {axis one} and {axis two}.
entries.guidance: Choose verified axes such as representation, supervision, data, decision rule, interaction regime, or deployment assumption.
entries.meaning: Organizes related approach families by explicit technical dimensions relevant to the present argument.

provenance.note: Original section-aware pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

To handle {challenge}, the model uses {technical choice}.
entries.guidance: Use the same challenge and component names throughout the Introduction, Method, and experiments. Avoid implying causal sufficiency without evidence.
entries.meaning: Maps one emphasized challenge to the corresponding design mechanism.

provenance.note: Original section-aware pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

The experiments test {main comparison}, {mechanism claim}, and {deployment boundary}.
entries.expression: Our contributions are evaluated through {research questions}.
entries.guidance: Replace the slot with two or three concrete questions or evaluation axes. Pair non-empirical contributions with theorems, resources, or analyses instead.
entries.meaning: Frames empirical contributions as questions that the Experiments section is designed to answer.

provenance.note: Original section-aware pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

Our analysis concerns {formal regime} and does not establish {broader guarantee}.
entries.expression: We focus on {scope}; {non-goal} remains outside the present study.
entries.guidance: Use for a material assumption or non-goal, especially when motivation is broader than evaluation. Keep it consistent with Limitations.
entries.meaning: States an explicit boundary that prevents an overbroad reading of the contribution.

This analysis motivates {design choice}, which targets {failure mode}.
entries.expression: Motivated by this observation, we design {mechanism} to {goal}.
entries.guidance: Ensure the antecedent observation directly motivates the mechanism. Name the technical goal rather than 'better performance.'
entries.meaning: Bridges a stated insight or empirical observation to the paper's design response.

provenance.note: Original section-aware pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.avoid: Avoid beginning from an expansive societal claim when the paper evaluates a narrower technical setting.

We consider {task} in the {offline, online, simulated, or real-system} setting.
entries.guidance: Specify the decision, observation, data, interaction, or deployment regime that makes the task operationally distinct.
entries.meaning: Defines the paper's task and setting before broader motivation or method details.

provenance.note: Original section-aware pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

The requirement for {resource} limits deployment in {setting}, where {constraint}.
entries.expression: This assumption becomes restrictive when {condition}, because {consequence}.
entries.guidance: State the assumption, triggering condition, and consequence explicitly. Support literature and empirical claims with primary evidence.
entries.meaning: Connects a verified method assumption to the condition under which it limits the target capability.

provenance.note: Original section-aware pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.expression: Latency is measured on {hardware} with {precision, batch, and timing boundary}.
entries.guidance: State warm-up, synchronization, repeats, input shape, preprocessing, action decoding, and whether the value is model-only or end to end.
entries.meaning: Defines the hardware and measurement boundary required to interpret latency.

provenance.note: Original experimental-writing pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

Lower {metric} indicates {meaning}; each value is averaged over {evaluation unit}.
entries.expression: Higher values of {metric} indicate {meaning}; results are averaged over {unit}.
entries.guidance: Use 'lower' where appropriate and name whether the unit is task, scene, episode, trial, seed, or example.
entries.meaning: Defines metric direction, interpretation, and the statistical unit used for aggregation.

provenance.note: Original experimental-writing pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.expression: A central challenge is to {objective} while {constraint}.

entries.meaning: Motivates a problem through a concrete objective–constraint tension.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

examples: Prior approaches differ primarily in how they {technical axis one} and whether they {technical axis two}.
entries.expression: Prior approaches differ primarily in {axis one} and {axis two}.
entries.guidance: Choose axes that expose meaningful assumptions or design choices, then place representative methods along them with citations.
entries.meaning: Organizes related work by technical comparison axes instead of paper-by-paper chronology.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Avoid claiming complete novelty merely because the exact combination has not appeared.
examples: Our setting is most closely related to {method family}, but differs in its assumption of {assumption} and its objective of {objective}.
entries.expression: Our setting is most closely related to {family}, but differs in {assumption or objective}.
entries.guidance: Name the closest family before the distinction. The difference should be technically consequential, not cosmetic.
entries.meaning: Positions the present work relative to the nearest literature family.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

examples: {method} improves mean {metric} by {absolute or relative value} over {baseline} under the {protocol} protocol.
entries.guidance: State whether the value is absolute or relative, and match the aggregation and uncertainty used in the table.
entries.meaning: Reports a quantified comparison with its baseline and protocol.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.guidance: Also state reset procedure, intervention policy, trial independence, task allocation, and the denominator used for success rate.
entries.meaning: Defines the trial count and success criterion for a physical or deployed-system evaluation.

provenance.note: Original experimental-writing pattern authored after the section-writing audit.

entries.meaning: Acknowledges a valid concern while delimiting what the current paper can support.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.meaning: Answers a reviewer question immediately and then points to evidence.

entries.meaning: Acknowledges unclear presentation and states the intended meaning directly.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.
