entries.guidance: Identify the state–action distribution and downstream quantity affected. Separate model bias from finite-sample variance and generic policy-estimation error.
entries.meaning: Distortion in policy learning or planning caused by systematic discrepancies between learned model transitions and the environment transitions relevant to the evaluated policy.

provenance.note: Field-standard term indexed from analyses of learned-model usage in policy optimization.

entries.avoid: Do not label every performance gap as model exploitation without showing that optimization interacts with model error.

entries.guidance: Use the term when the optimizer or policy actively seeks regions where model errors are favorable. Support the diagnosis with real-environment evaluation or an appropriate uncertainty/error analysis.
entries.meaning: A failure mode in which optimization selects actions that look favorable under an inaccurate learned model but do not yield the predicted outcomes in the real environment.

provenance.note: Field-standard failure-mode terminology synthesized from model-based RL analyses.

entries.avoid: Do not use MPC as a synonym for any policy that consumes model predictions.

entries.meaning: A control strategy that repeatedly optimizes a finite-horizon action sequence using a model, executes an initial portion, and replans from the new state.

provenance.note: Canonical term indexed from linked primary papers; examples are original.

entries.meaning: A component that maps a latent state to a distribution over observations or reconstructs observation-space outputs.

provenance.note: Canonical term indexed from linked primary papers; examples are original.

entries.avoid: Do not call a single open-loop plan receding-horizon control.

entries.meaning: Planning in which a finite-horizon solution is repeatedly recomputed as new observations become available.

provenance.note: Canonical term indexed from linked primary papers; examples are original.

entries.avoid: Do not claim that stochastic latents capture calibrated uncertainty unless calibration is evaluated.

provenance.note: Canonical term indexed from linked primary papers; examples are original.

entries.meaning: A sampling procedure that propagates multiple hypothetical trajectories through a probabilistic dynamics model to approximate distributions over future outcomes.

entries.avoid: Do not claim perfect decomposition merely because a network predicts a variance and an ensemble produces disagreement.

provenance.note: Independent scope guidance based on the uncertainty treatment in PETS.

entries.avoid: Do not use a low one-step reconstruction loss as sufficient evidence of long-horizon planning fidelity.
examples: We evaluate one-step prediction under {protocol} and multi-step consistency over {horizons} under {rollout mode}.

entries.guidance: Report horizon-conditioned errors or task outcomes and distinguish teacher-forced, open-loop, and replanned predictions.
entries.meaning: One-step loss measures local transition fit, whereas multi-step consistency tests whether iterated or direct predictions remain coherent over decision-relevant horizons.

provenance.note: Evaluation distinction consolidated from recent predictive-model work.

promotion_decisions.rationale: The state–action occupancy-measure concept is field-standard, reusable across policy optimization and constrained or general-utility RL, and was absent from the normalized corpus.
The paper operationalizes egocentric embodied cognition as a benchmark, while its reusable concepts are already covered by the egocentric-observation and multimodal-perception records.
The continual-learning mechanisms are method-specific, whereas the transferable technical language is already represented by model-based RL, learned dynamics, and world-model records.
Average-reward RL is a stable continuing-task formulation with recurring theoretical and experimental usage, but the corpus previously covered only discounted or generic return language.

Room-tour reconstruction and instruction generation are dataset-specific contributions; the reusable writing concepts map cleanly to vision-and-language navigation, egocentric observation, and explicit generalization axes.
The paper's method name and sparse-memory design are specific, while embodied future prediction, video world modeling, and action chunks already have normalized reusable records.
Text-aware feature selection is a method-specific mechanism; the paper directly supports the existing VLA definition and the need to name held-out object and environment generalization axes.

Time-reversal augmentation is a valid paper-specific contribution, but the reviewed wording does not add a broadly reusable concept beyond existing forward/inverse dynamics and sample-efficiency records.

The online feedback mechanism is specific to the proposed method; existing rapid-online-adaptation and VLN records already express the reusable concept with the required adaptation and navigation qualifiers.
The mixture-of-experts architecture is method-specific, while the transferable formulation is already captured by offline RL and return-conditioned sequence-modeling records.

limitations: This is a calibration sample, not a statistical estimate of venue style or acceptance determinants.

ICLR papers remain represented in the 300-paper metadata and abstract study but were not included in this full-text sample because the official PDF endpoint rejected automated retrieval during the audit.
Document-level phrase detection can miss wording because PDF text extraction is imperfect and cannot assess scientific validity.
No extracted paper text is redistributed, and all reusable templates are independently authored.
section_study.method: A deterministic, balanced sample of official full-paper PDFs was converted to local text for document-level structural analysis. The repository retains only source IDs and aggregate counts, not paper prose.
observations: Section headings vary substantially, so protocols should specify functional moves rather than enforce one heading sequence.
Baseline, implementation, evaluation, ablation, and display-referencing moves recur, but their presence alone does not establish comparison fairness or reproducibility.
Result paragraphs commonly point to a display before stating an observation; the library therefore requires a quantified comparison and a calibrated interpretation after that pointer.
Abstract and Introduction claims must be checked against experiment scope instead of being optimized independently for persuasive force.
section_study.scope: Forty papers from the audited 2021–2025 collection were sampled across reinforcement learning, embodied AI, world models, and vision-language-action models to calibrate Abstract, Introduction, Experiments, analysis, and table protocols.

avoid: Opening with an unverifiable claim that the broad field is fundamentally important.
Using 'novel', 'effective', 'superior', or 'state-of-the-art' as substitutes for a technical contribution and verified result.
Listing modules without explaining the insight that connects them.
Adding citations, results, or deployment claims not present in the completed paper.
inputs: One-sentence problem and evaluated scope.
The specific unresolved limitation or challenge addressed by this paper.
The paper's core insight and the mechanism that realizes it.
Verified principal evidence, including benchmark, metric, comparison, statistic, and uncertainty when available.
Assumptions, deployment boundary, or evaluated generalization axis that materially limits the claim.
guides.label: Abstract: claim-aligned empirical summary

checks: Map every proposed abstract claim to a section, theorem, table, or figure in the paper.
Remove a claim if the mapped evidence does not support its comparison set or generalization scope.
Keep aspirational motivation grammatically distinct from achieved results.
moves.label: Build an abstract claim ledger

checks: Name the task or setting before the broad application motivation.
Describe a concrete assumption, failure mode, resource bottleneck, or missing capability rather than calling prior work insufficient.
Do not claim priority or novelty unless independently verified.
moves.label: State the problem and precise gap

checks: State what makes the approach work conceptually, then name the mechanism.
Do not enumerate low-level modules that do not affect the paper-level contribution.
moves.label: Connect insight to mechanism

checks: Prefer one decision-relevant verified result over 'extensive experiments demonstrate'.
Distinguish absolute change from relative change and percentage points.
End with the supported implication or boundary, not a universal superiority claim.
moves.label: Report evidence with scope

guides.purpose: Produce a compact summary whose problem, contribution, evidence, and scope exactly match the completed paper.

templates.name: Empirical method paper
sequence: Task and operational context.
Specific limitation under a named setting or assumption.
Core insight.
Method and mechanism.
Verified principal comparison with evaluation scope.
Supported implication or explicit boundary.
templates.when: The main contribution is a method evaluated on benchmarks, simulation, or real systems.

templates.name: Resource or benchmark paper
sequence: Capability that cannot currently be measured well.
Coverage or validity gap in existing resources.
What the new resource contains and how it is constructed.
What diagnostic dimensions or tasks it enables.
Verified baseline findings and what they reveal.
Access, scope, or limitation statement.
templates.when: The main contribution is a dataset, environment, benchmark, or evaluation protocol.

templates.name: Theory-led paper
sequence: Problem and formal setting.
Limitation of existing guarantees.
Main result with its assumptions.
Key proof or algorithmic idea at a high level.
Implication relative to the prior bound or setting.
Empirical evidence only if it is actually part of the contribution.
templates.when: The main contribution is a theorem, guarantee, bound, or analysis.

guides.use_when: Drafting or revising an AI-paper abstract after the methods and principal results are known.
verification: The abstract uses the same task, method name, metric names, and comparison direction as the body.
Every number matches the final table or theorem, including units, denominator, and aggregation.
No conclusion extends beyond the evaluated datasets, tasks, embodiments, shifts, or assumptions.
The target venue's current length, paragraph, citation, and formatting rules were checked separately.

avoid: A universal six-paragraph requirement; use functional moves and merge them when the argument benefits.
A straw-man progression from a deliberately weak 'naive' solution to the proposed method.
Chronological paper listing, unverified 'first' claims, and generic importance claims.
Contribution bullets that mix a task definition, one module, and a result at incompatible levels.
inputs: Paper type: method, new problem or setting, resource, empirical study, or theory.
Task definition, relevant application stakes, and intended reader prerequisites.
Closest approach families and the verified axes on which they differ.
The exact limitation addressed, including its assumptions and practical consequence.
Core insight, design elements, contribution claims, and the experiment or theorem supporting each claim.
guides.label: Introduction: limitation–insight–evidence alignment

checks: Define the operational task before expanding to broader motivation.
Use a concrete running scenario only when it is real and technically representative.
Avoid claiming that all prior work shares one weakness.
moves.label: Establish scope and problem

checks: Group work by representation, supervision, data, decision mechanism, interaction regime, or deployment assumption.
Use only verified literature relationships and reserve detailed chronology for Related Work.
Make the comparison axis explicit before stating the limitation.
moves.label: Map closest approaches

checks: Name the condition under which the limitation matters.
Separate lack of evaluation from evidence of failure.
Do not turn a design difference into a defect without evidence.
moves.label: State gap and consequence

checks: State the key insight before the component list.
Map each emphasized challenge to a design choice.
Explain the causal claim only as strongly as the design and analysis allow.
moves.label: Bridge insight to design

checks: Write parallel contributions at the same abstraction level.
Pair each empirical contribution with a named evaluation question or display.
Replace 'extensive experiments' with the evaluated axes and principal finding.
moves.label: Pair contributions with evidence

checks: State assumptions or non-goals that prevent an overbroad reading.
Keep the boundary consistent with the Limitations and Experiments sections.
moves.label: Close with scope

guides.purpose: Build an argument that moves from a scoped problem to a verified gap, design insight, contribution, and evidence without relying on a fixed paragraph count.

templates.name: Technique paper
sequence: Operational task and stakes.
Closest method families and relevant comparison axes.
Limitation under a named condition.
Key insight and method overview.
Contribution–evidence pairs.
Supported scope or non-goal.
templates.when: A new method addresses a known task.

templates.name: New setting or resource
sequence: Missing capability or evaluation need.
Why existing settings fail to measure it.
Definition and design principles of the new setting.
Coverage, validity, and diagnostic axes.
Baseline findings and remaining gap.
Availability and boundary.
templates.when: The paper primarily introduces a task, dataset, benchmark, or problem formulation.

templates.name: Theory or analysis paper
sequence: Formal problem and why it matters.
Known results and the unresolved regime.
Main insight or analytical device.
Principal result and assumptions.
Consequences and evidence.
Limits of the analysis.
templates.when: The main contribution is explanatory or formal rather than architectural.

guides.use_when: Planning, drafting, or restructuring an AI-paper Introduction.
verification: Construct a matrix from limitation to challenge, design choice, contribution, and supporting experiment or theorem.
Check every literature statement against primary papers rather than the library or another paper's Related Work.
Ensure contribution wording matches the Abstract and does not exceed the evidence summarized later.
Read the Introduction once without citations: the logical bridge should remain clear.

avoid: Calling a study comprehensive because it contains many datasets without covering the paper's actual claim axes.
Reporting only favorable seeds, tasks, checkpoints, qualitative examples, or hyperparameter ranges.
Attributing a gain to one component from a tiny or noisy ablation difference.
Treating simulation success, offline metrics, open-loop prediction, and closed-loop deployment as interchangeable evidence.
Using an appendix pointer to replace the minimum protocol information needed to interpret a main result.

checks: Separate environment interactions, gradient updates, episodes, wall-clock time, replay ratio, and offline transition count; never report them as one generic sample budget.
Name the environment version, observation and action interfaces, horizon or termination rule, reward convention, and any score normalization reference.
Report evaluation episodes per seed, independent training seeds, aggregation across tasks, uncertainty, and the checkpoint-selection protocol.
For offline RL, describe dataset provenance, behavior-policy mixture, support or coverage diagnostics, and whether any online interaction or evaluation data informed tuning.

checks: Separate one-step prediction, multi-step open-loop rollout, closed-loop planning, and downstream policy evidence; none is a substitute for another.
Report prediction target, latent or observation space, action conditioning, context length, rollout horizon, replanning interval, and stochastic sampling procedure.

checks: Name simulator and real-system conditions separately, including platform, sensing, workspace, control loop, safety constraints, and sim-to-real differences.
Define a trial, reset, intervention, timeout, partial completion, and success denominator; report per-task counts and uncertainty rather than only a pooled percentage.
Describe demonstrations by task, trajectory, timestep, operator, embodiment, and collection policy when these affect data comparability.
Make held-out objects, scenes, tasks, instructions, users, and embodiments distinct generalization axes and disclose selection on any held-out condition.
domain_overlays.label: Embodied AI and robot learning

checks: Report pretraining and robot data mixtures, embodiment-specific heads, action representation, prediction horizon, execution horizon, and feedback or replanning interval.
Separate model-query latency, action-chunk generation time, effective control frequency, end-to-end task time, and hardware or precision conditions.
State whether evaluation is open-loop prediction, closed-loop control, simulation, or physical deployment and avoid transferring conclusions across those regimes.

inputs: Empirical claim list and one research question per claim.
Datasets, tasks, splits, environments, embodiments, populations, and held-out units.
Metrics with direction, units, denominator, aggregation unit, and decision relevance.
Baseline implementations, training data, pretraining, tuning, parameter, compute, and interaction budgets.
Seeds or trials, checkpoint and hyperparameter selection protocol, uncertainty statistic, and statistical tests when used.
Hardware, software versions, training and evaluation compute, real-system safety constraints, and failure records.

checks: For every claim, record research question, comparison axis, protocol, metric, display, and allowed interpretation.
Place claim-critical evidence in the main paper when the venue warns that reviewers may not consult appendices.
Remove experiments that do not test a stated claim or label them exploratory.
moves.label: Create the claim–evidence matrix

checks: Describe task, data provenance, split construction, held-out unit, and evaluation population.
For embodied work, distinguish simulation from real-system trials and name the control loop, intervention, reset, and success denominator.
For RL, distinguish environment steps, gradient steps, episodes, wall-clock time, and offline data size.
moves.label: Define evaluation scope

checks: State whether higher or lower is better, the unit, and the averaging unit.
Report the number of independent seeds, runs, scenes, tasks, episodes, or trials and avoid treating correlated samples as independent.
Name mean, median, standard deviation, standard error, confidence interval, or percentile explicitly.
moves.label: Define metrics and statistical unit

checks: Record implementation source, version, reproduction changes, and tuning protocol for each baseline.
Disclose material differences in pretraining data, model scale, supervision, compute, and interaction budget.
Do not bold a result as best when protocols are not comparable.
moves.label: Establish baseline fairness

checks: Lead each result paragraph with the question or comparison axis.
Point to the display, quantify the relevant difference, state consistency or exceptions, then give a calibrated interpretation.
Report null, negative, unstable, or adverse results when they bear on the claim.
moves.label: Answer the primary research questions

checks: Use ablation for component or mechanism claims, generalization for named shifts, robustness for named perturbations, and efficiency for named resources.
Add sensitivity or scaling analysis when a conclusion depends on a chosen hyperparameter or scale.
Include qualitative examples and failure cases when metrics conceal behavior relevant to deployment.

checks: Provide enough implementation and evaluation detail to reconstruct the reported protocol.
State code, data, simulator, benchmark, and model availability only as actually provided.

guides.purpose: Design and write an experimental section in which each major empirical claim is tested under an explicit protocol and bounded interpretation.

templates.name: Standard empirical evaluation
sequence: Research questions or evaluation goals.
Tasks, datasets, splits, and metrics.
Baselines and fairness controls.
Implementation, selection, and statistical protocol.
Main results organized by research question.
Ablation or mechanism analysis.
Generalization, robustness, efficiency, qualitative behavior, or failures only as claim-relevant.
Scope summary and appendix pointers.

Matched baselines and deployment latency.
Per-task result counts with uncertainty.
Representative failures and safety-relevant limitations.

templates.name: Theory with supporting experiments
sequence: Question tied to the theorem or assumption.
Synthetic setting that isolates the predicted behavior.
Metric and parameter regime.
Comparison with the predicted trend or bound.
Realistic setting, if used, clearly separated from proof.
Conditions where empirical behavior departs from the theory.

verification: Every main empirical claim has a visible row in the claim–evidence matrix.
Numbers and method labels agree across Abstract, Experiments, captions, tables, figures, and appendix.
Absolute changes, relative changes, and percentage-point changes are labeled correctly.
Comparison conclusions name the matched and unmatched resources.
Metric direction, units, denominator, number of runs, and uncertainty are recoverable without guessing.
Supplement placement follows current venue rules; critical evidence is not hidden behind an optional review path.

avoid: Beginning every sentence with 'Table X shows' and paraphrasing the full table.
Using 'because' or 'due to' when an ablation only establishes association.
Describing a one-benchmark gain as general improvement.
Calling overlapping error bars a significance test or non-overlapping bars proof of a mechanism.
inputs: The research question and comparison axis.
Exact table or figure location and verified values.
Aggregation, uncertainty, and statistical unit.
Expected mechanism, plausible alternatives, exceptions, and failure cases.
guides.label: Experimental analysis: evidence before interpretation

checks: Point to the display and identify the rows, columns, or trend relevant to the question.
Quantify the difference in the metric's natural unit and distinguish relative from absolute change.
State whether the pattern is consistent across tasks, datasets, seeds, scales, or shifts.
moves.label: State the evidence

checks: Use 'is consistent with' or 'suggests' for a mechanism not directly identified.
Name alternative explanations such as scale, data, tuning, or compute when they remain uncontrolled.
Do not equate lack of statistical significance with equivalence.
moves.label: Calibrate interpretation

checks: Identify settings where the advantage diminishes, reverses, or becomes unstable.
State quality–efficiency, robustness–accuracy, or data–compute trade-offs explicitly.
Connect a failure case to the claim it limits.
moves.label: Report boundary and trade-off

guides.purpose: Turn verified results into precise analysis paragraphs without merely narrating a table or overstating a mechanism.

templates.name: Main result paragraph
sequence: Question and display pointer.
Quantified main comparison.
Consistency across relevant settings.
Calibrated explanation.
Exception, uncertainty, or trade-off.
templates.when: A table or figure answers one primary research question.

templates.name: Ablation paragraph
sequence: Component question and full-model anchor.
Matched variant comparison.
Magnitude relative to uncertainty.
Interaction or non-additivity if modules are coupled.
Narrow conclusion about contribution, not universal necessity.
templates.when: Variants test components, losses, data sources, or design choices.

templates.name: Failure analysis paragraph
sequence: Failure taxonomy and denominator.
Most frequent or consequential category.
Condition associated with the failure.
Plausible explanation separated from observed fact.
Implication for scope, deployment, or future evaluation.
templates.when: Failures are categorized qualitatively or quantitatively.

guides.use_when: Writing main-result, ablation, robustness, efficiency, or failure-analysis paragraphs after displays are finalized.
verification: Every adjective such as consistent, substantial, stable, or efficient is tied to a visible statistic or named condition.
The prose does not repeat every cell; it selects the comparison that answers the stated question.
Interpretations preserve uncertainty and do not exceed the intervention or control structure.
Negative and anomalous results are not silently omitted from the described trend.

avoid: Using decorative color or mandatory best/second-best colors.
Mixing percentages and fractions in one metric without explicit units.
Averaging metrics with incompatible scales into an unexplained overall score.
Packing setup details into tiny cells that reviewers cannot read.
inputs: Research question and comparison axis.
Source data, analysis script, and exact mapping from cells to outputs.
Metric direction, units, denominator, aggregation, uncertainty, and number of independent runs.
Protocol differences in data, pretraining, compute, interaction, tuning, hardware, or evaluation.
guides.label: Tables: common construction and reporting standard

checks: A reader should be able to state what comparison the table answers in one sentence.
Split unrelated settings or metrics when grouping obscures the decision.
moves.label: Assign one primary question

checks: Name task, dataset or environment, split, and evaluation setting.
Define metric direction, units, aggregation, uncertainty, number of runs, abbreviations, and emphasis rules.
State consequential protocol differences or point to a precise footnote.
moves.label: Write a self-contained caption

checks: Group baselines by method family or protocol and keep row labels stable across tables.
Order columns by task, shift, or metric logic rather than by favorable outcome.
Use consistent precision justified by measurement uncertainty.
moves.label: Structure rows and columns

checks: Do not use color as the only cue; define bold, underline, symbols, and arrows.
Distinguish zero, missing, not reported, and not applicable.
Prefer restrained horizontal rules and avoid vertical-rule clutter.
moves.label: Use accessible, unambiguous encoding

checks: Every cited value and ranking in prose matches the table.
Cells trace to source data and transformations.
Emphasis compares only rows under a defensible common protocol.
moves.label: Reconcile table and prose

guides.purpose: Make each table answer one research question with enough protocol information to interpret every comparison.

templates.name: General quantitative caption
sequence: What is evaluated and where.
Protocol or split.
Metric names with arrows and units.
Statistic, uncertainty, and number of independent runs.
Meaning of emphasis and missing-value symbols.
Material protocol exceptions.

guides.use_when: Designing or auditing any quantitative experimental table.
verification: The table remains interpretable when separated from the surrounding paragraph.
Bold or underline never implies a fair ranking across incomparable protocols.
Missing values use a documented symbol and are not encoded as zero.
The table is legible in grayscale and at final publication size.
No significance marker appears without a verified test, comparison, and correction policy when applicable.

avoid: Ranking a larger pretrained model against a from-scratch baseline as if architecture were the only difference.
Selecting baseline numbers from incompatible papers or evaluation protocols without a clear separator.
Using average rank or an overall score to conceal regressions on important tasks.
inputs: Proposed variants and verified baseline set.
Task or dataset groups and principal decision-relevant metrics.
Pretraining, data, model-scale, compute, interaction, and tuning differences.
Per-run values or verified aggregate statistics.

checks: Separate methods that use extra data, pretraining, privileged inputs, larger models, or different interaction budgets.
Include the strongest relevant baseline that can be evaluated fairly; explain omissions.
moves.label: Group comparable baselines

checks: Lead with the metric that answers the research question.
Add resource or safety metrics when the main claim depends on them.
Use an overall average only when component metrics are commensurate and the weighting is defined.
moves.label: Prioritize claim-relevant metrics

checks: Apply best-result emphasis only within comparable row groups.
Do not hide uncertainty to make a small ranking difference appear decisive.
moves.label: Define ranking scope

guides.purpose: Compare the proposed method with relevant baselines while making protocol equivalence and principal metrics visible.

templates.name: Methods by tasks or datasets
sequence: Rows: method families, then the proposed method and named variants.
Columns: protocol flags, task–metric groups, then a justified aggregate.
Caption: setting, split, metric directions, aggregation, runs, emphasis, and extra-resource flags.
Footnotes: implementation or protocol exceptions.

guides.use_when: The central table supports the paper's primary empirical comparison.
verification: Every baseline row identifies whether results are reproduced, taken from a source, or rerun.
The same checkpoint-selection and evaluation budget are used or differences are disclosed.
The prose quantifies the primary comparison instead of only claiming the best rank.

avoid: Calling a hyperparameter sweep an ablation without defining the design claim.
Removing multiple coupled components in one row and attributing the change to one of them.
Reporting only the best seed or one favorable task.
inputs: Full model and the claim attached to each component or design choice.
Matched training data, initialization, optimization, compute, evaluation, and seeds.
Known or plausible component interactions.
Per-variant statistics and uncertainty.

checks: Use the full method as an explicit anchor.
Change one factor at a time unless the table explicitly tests an interaction.
Retune only under a declared common policy; disabling a component may change the best optimization settings.

checks: Add factorial or paired variants when components are theoretically coupled.
Do not add single-component drops as if effects were additive when interactions are expected.

checks: Compare the effect magnitude with run-to-run uncertainty.
Conclude contribution under the tested configuration, not universal necessity.
Report removals that improve a metric and discuss the trade-off.
moves.label: Bound the conclusion

guides.purpose: Test component, loss, data, or design claims with matched variants and conclusions no stronger than the intervention supports.

guides.use_when: A table compares the full method with controlled variants.
verification: All variants use the declared matched protocol.
The table includes the actual full method used for the main result.
Component names are identical in Method, table, caption, and prose.
Ablation claims do not rely on differences smaller than the reported uncertainty without further analysis.

avoid: Labeling a random example split as novel-task or novel-environment generalization.
Reporting only shifted results and hiding degradation in the reference condition.
Tuning on the test shift while describing it as unseen.
inputs: Training distribution and exact held-out unit.
Reference, shifted, and severity conditions.
Metric, denominator, seeds or trials, and uncertainty.
Whether model selection used any shifted-condition information.

checks: Name what is unseen and how it was withheld.
Separate interpolation, compositional recombination, domain shift, and open-set evaluation.

checks: Report in-distribution or seen-condition performance beside shifted performance.
Make accuracy–robustness trade-offs visible.

checks: State which data selected hyperparameters and checkpoints.
Do not call a condition held out if it influenced tuning or prompt selection.

guides.purpose: Make the training–evaluation shift or perturbation explicit and report performance across both reference and shifted conditions.

templates.name: Training versus shifted evaluation

Columns: seen reference, each named shift or severity, and a defined gap metric if useful.

Analysis: shifted-condition difference, reference trade-off, consistency, and residual failure.

guides.use_when: Claims concern unseen tasks, objects, environments, embodiments, distributions, corruptions, or perturbations.
verification: The held-out definition can be reconstructed from the caption or referenced setup.
The term out-of-distribution is tied to a specific changed variable.
Any robustness average states the perturbation set and weighting.
The conclusion does not generalize beyond the sampled shift.

avoid: Calling a method efficient solely because it has fewer parameters.
Comparing latency measured on different hardware without separation.
Reporting throughput at a large batch as single-sample latency.
Ignoring preprocessing, communication, simulator, or action-decoding time when it dominates deployment.
inputs: Quality metric and the exact resource axis.
Hardware, software, precision, batch size, sequence length, input resolution, and concurrency.
Training data or interaction budget and stopping rule.
Warm-up, synchronization, preprocessing, and measurement window.

checks: Distinguish parameters, FLOPs, accelerator-hours, wall-clock time, peak memory, latency, throughput, energy, environment steps, and demonstrations.
Do not use sample efficiency when only optimization steps are reduced.

checks: State hardware, precision, batch, input shape, warm-up, synchronization, and included preprocessing.
For robot policies, distinguish model inference latency from end-to-end control-loop frequency.
moves.label: Fix the measurement protocol

checks: Report quality and resource in the same table or linked display.
Compare at matched quality, matched resource, or present the Pareto frontier.

guides.purpose: Report quality jointly with the resource that defines efficiency under a reproducible measurement protocol.

templates.name: Deployment profile
sequence: Rows: methods and deployment variants.
Columns: quality, parameters, peak memory, latency and/or throughput, and control rate when relevant.
Caption: hardware, precision, batch, input, timing boundary, repeats, and uncertainty.
Analysis: matched-quality or matched-resource comparison and trade-off.
templates.when: Methods are compared for inference or control deployment.

guides.use_when: Claims concern sample, compute, memory, parameter, latency, throughput, energy, or deployment efficiency.
verification: Resource units and measurement boundaries are explicit.
Training and inference resources are not mixed in one undefined efficiency claim.
Reported throughput and latency use compatible batch and concurrency assumptions.
Any deployment claim is checked against the actual real-time requirement.

avoid: Showing a narrow range centered on the selected value without rationale.
Choosing a different best hyperparameter for every test task without disclosing the oracle.
Calling a three-point sweep a scaling law.
Hiding unstable or failed settings.
inputs: Parameter or scale, unit, candidate range, and rationale.
Selection set, selection objective, and whether the sweep was planned or exploratory.
Matched factors held constant across values.
Per-value metric, resource, runs, and uncertainty.

checks: Report the full evaluated range in a meaningful linear or logarithmic order.
Mark the chosen default and state how it was selected.
Include boundary values that can reveal collapse when feasible.

checks: State data, optimization, compute, evaluation, and seeds held constant.
When scale changes compute, report the changed resource rather than implying a one-factor intervention.

checks: Report stability range, monotonicity, saturation, reversal, or instability.
Separate a tuning optimum from evidence for the proposed mechanism.
moves.label: Describe sensitivity, not just optimum

guides.purpose: Show how conclusions change with a hyperparameter, data scale, model scale, horizon, or evaluation budget without cherry-picking.

templates.name: Parameter or scale sweep
sequence: Rows: ordered parameter or scale values with the default marked.
Columns: claim-relevant metric, uncertainty, and changed resource.
Caption: range, selection protocol, controls, runs, and default marker.
Analysis: trend, stable region, chosen point, and exception.
templates.when: One ordered variable is varied.

guides.use_when: A claim or design choice depends on a selected value, range, or scale.
verification: All evaluated values are reported or omissions are explained.
Test-set performance did not select the final value unless explicitly declared as exploratory.
Scaling conclusions separate benefits of model size, data, and compute where the design permits.
The prose discusses the trend and uncertainty rather than only the maximum cell.

avoid: One sentence per paper with no cross-paper synthesis.
Citation clusters whose individual sources do not support the whole sentence.
Describing prior work only through limitations while omitting its intended setting or strength.
Using temporal recency as a proxy for relevance, quality, or novelty.
inputs: The exact task, setting, and claim that the literature discussion must contextualize.
Verified primary papers with bibliographic metadata and notes tied to specific passages.
A small set of organizing families and explicit comparison axes such as objective, supervision, data regime, assumptions, compute, or deployment setting.
The present paper's factual relationship to each relevant family, including shared assumptions and material differences.
guides.label: Related Work: evidence-verified synthesis and positioning

checks: Open every primary paper used for a definition, historical claim, method characterization, or comparison.
Record what the cited passage supports and do not infer absent limitations from silence.
Use the library's source IDs only as navigation; never treat a corpus summary as the citation evidence.
moves.label: Verify the literature evidence

checks: Group papers by the technical choice that matters to this paper rather than by arbitrary chronology.
State the comparison axis before naming examples from a family.
Separate families that solve different problem settings instead of ranking them together.
moves.label: Build a task-relevant taxonomy

checks: Describe a recurring approach, then identify a verified assumption, mechanism, or scope difference.
Make the subject of every evaluative statement explicit: method, dataset, protocol, or result.
Distinguish reported evidence from the authors' interpretation and from this paper's synthesis.
moves.label: Synthesize similarities and differences

checks: State what is shared with prior work before the differentiating axis.
Name the changed assumption, supervision, data, mechanism, evaluation, or deployment constraint.
Do not imply superiority unless a verified comparable experiment supports it.
moves.label: Position the present work precisely

guides.purpose: Organize verified primary papers into problem-relevant families, compare them on explicit axes, and locate the present work without paper-by-paper narration or unsupported priority claims.

templates.name: Taxonomy-first synthesis
sequence: Define the shared task and organizing axis.
Describe the first family and its operative assumption.
Contrast the next family on the same axis.
Synthesize the unresolved boundary across families.
Position the present work on that boundary.
templates.when: Several approach families address a common task under different assumptions.

templates.name: Concept evolution
sequence: State the original formulation or capability with a primary source.
Describe the verified change introduced by subsequent work.
Compare the resulting families on a stable axis rather than merely listing years.
Identify the remaining problem addressed here.
templates.when: Chronology is scientifically meaningful because later work changes a specific assumption or capability.

guides.use_when: Planning, drafting, or revising an AI-paper Related Work section or a focused literature-positioning paragraph.
verification: Every citation exists, has been opened, and supports the adjacent proposition at the stated scope.
Every comparison names a common axis and avoids ranking incompatible protocols.
Definitions are paraphrases unless a short quotation is explicitly marked and permitted.
The section represents close alternatives fairly, including assumptions that favor the present method.
No claim uses latest, first, only, most, or state-of-the-art without a separately verified comparison set.

avoid: Using intuitive prose in place of an operational definition.
Introducing modules as a list without interfaces or design rationale.
Hiding optimization, selection, or inference details behind 'we follow standard practice'.
Claiming a component causes an improvement when the design only establishes correlation.
inputs: Operational task definition, notation, inputs, outputs, supervision, and assumptions.
Component graph with tensor or state interfaces and the purpose of each component.
Objectives with signs, weights, estimators, gradient boundaries, and optimization schedule.
Training-data flow and deployment-time procedure, including what information is available at each stage.
Claim-to-mechanism map and material compute, latency, memory, or sampling requirements.
guides.label: Method: executable specification and design rationale

checks: Define every symbol before or at first use and state tensor, sequence, or state semantics when ambiguity matters.
Separate training-only supervision or privileged information from inference-time inputs.
State assumptions and non-goals that limit what the formulation represents.
moves.label: Define the problem and information boundary

checks: For each component, state its input, output, transformation, and downstream consumer.
Explain why the component addresses a named failure mode or claim rather than only naming its architecture.
Keep notation and component names identical across text, equations, figures, pseudocode, and appendices.
moves.label: Specify components through interfaces

checks: Define each loss or reward term, coefficient, estimator, normalization, mask, and reduction.
State where gradients flow or stop and which parameters each term updates.
Distinguish the optimized surrogate from the scientific quantity it is intended to improve.
moves.label: Make the learning objective auditable

checks: Give an ordered training procedure with data sampling, update ratios, target updates, and selection protocol where relevant.
Give an ordered inference or control procedure with state, decoding, replanning, stopping, and timing boundaries.
Surface stochastic choices, seeds, search budgets, or external modules that affect reproducibility.
moves.label: Separate training and inference procedures

guides.purpose: Describe the problem formulation, components, objective, training procedure, and inference behavior precisely enough that a technically competent reader can reconstruct the method and test each claimed mechanism.

templates.name: Model–objective–procedure
sequence: Problem formulation and notation.
System overview and component interfaces.
Representation or prediction modules.
Training objectives and optimization.
Inference or control procedure.
Complexity, assumptions, and implementation-critical details.
templates.when: A learned architecture is the main contribution.

templates.name: Algorithmic procedure
sequence: Formal setting and objective.
Core update or search rule.
Estimator, approximation, and stopping conditions.
Pseudocode with all externally chosen quantities defined.
Computational requirements and applicable guarantees.
templates.when: The contribution is primarily an update rule, planner, optimizer, or decision procedure.

guides.use_when: Planning, drafting, or auditing an AI-paper Method section, algorithm description, or implementation-facing formulation.
verification: A reader can trace every input to every output without guessing an unstated module or data source.
Equations, pseudocode, diagrams, and prose use consistent notation and ordering.
Train-time and test-time information, computation, and model variants are explicitly separated.
Every mechanism claim has a corresponding experiment, theorem, diagnostic, or explicitly limited interpretation.
Implementation details that materially affect the comparison are in the main text or clearly routed appendix.

avoid: Generic statements that more data, compute, or future research may help.
Presenting a missing experiment as evidence of likely success or failure.
Minimizing a consequential failure because it occurs outside the average benchmark case.
Adding a limitation that contradicts the paper's main claim without reconciling the scope.
inputs: The paper's claims and the exact evidence supporting each claim.
Untested datasets, tasks, shifts, embodiments, populations, or deployment conditions that a reader might otherwise infer.
Observed failures, null results, sensitivity, safety concerns, and resource requirements.
Assumptions in the formulation, data, annotations, simulator, metrics, or evaluation protocol.
guides.label: Limitations: evidence boundary and consequential failure modes

checks: Name the evaluated axis and the nearest unsupported extrapolation.
Distinguish not evaluated, evaluated with a null result, and observed failure.
Use calibrated modality so uncertainty is not converted into a negative result.
moves.label: Bound each claim

checks: State the condition under which the failure occurs and the observable consequence.
Connect the boundary to a data, model, objective, protocol, or deployment mechanism when evidence permits.
Identify who or what is affected when the limitation has safety, fairness, or operational consequences.
moves.label: Describe mechanism and consequence

checks: Describe existing safeguards or diagnostics as implemented facts.
Label proposed mitigations as future work and do not imply they are validated.
Prioritize limitations that materially change interpretation over generic statements that all methods could make.
moves.label: Separate current mitigation from future work

guides.purpose: State where the evidence, assumptions, resources, and deployment conditions stop supporting the paper's claims, and identify concrete failure modes without generic disclaimers.

templates.name: Empirical boundary
sequence: Supported claim and evaluated scope.
Nearest untested or failed condition.
Observed evidence or reason for uncertainty.
Effect on interpretation or deployment.
Current mitigation and clearly labeled future validation.
templates.when: The main limitation is incomplete evaluation or a measured failure region.

templates.name: Assumption or resource boundary
sequence: Required assumption or resource.
Where it enters the method or evaluation.
What changes when it is violated or unavailable.
Scope of claims that remain valid.
templates.when: Performance relies on information, data, compute, hardware, or a formal assumption.

guides.use_when: Drafting a Limitations section, failure-boundary discussion, broader-impact caveat, or scoped response to an untested setting.
verification: Every limitation is specific enough to suggest a test, affected claim, or deployment decision.
Observed failures, null results, and untested settings are linguistically distinct.
The section does not introduce evidence or causal explanations absent from the paper.
Resource and data limitations include units, scale, provenance, or access conditions where relevant.
Safety-relevant limitations are not hidden behind vague future-work language.

avoid: Repeating the Abstract nearly verbatim.
Introducing a new experiment, citation, comparison, or technical mechanism.
Ending with an unbounded claim that the method opens broad new possibilities.
Omitting a trade-off that is necessary to interpret the main result.
inputs: Final problem statement and contribution claims.
Principal verified result or theoretical implication with its evaluation scope.
The most consequential limitation or next research question.
Any broader implication that follows directly from the paper rather than from aspiration.
guides.label: Conclusion: contribution–evidence–scope closure

checks: Restate the addressed problem at the same scope as the Introduction.
Name the core insight and contribution rather than listing every module.
Avoid copying the Abstract sentence by sentence.
moves.label: Synthesize problem and contribution

checks: State the principal verified finding and the setting in which it holds.
Retain exceptions, trade-offs, or uncertainty that materially affect the conclusion.
Do not upgrade a trend or benchmark result into a causal or universal claim.
moves.label: Close the claim with evidence

checks: Identify a specific remaining boundary or research direction grounded in the findings.
Separate demonstrated capability from plausible broader impact.
Introduce no new method detail, citation-dependent literature claim, or result.
moves.label: End with a bounded implication

guides.purpose: Close the paper by restating the solved problem, core contribution, principal verified evidence, and remaining boundary without adding new claims or repeating the abstract verbatim.

templates.name: Empirical paper closure
sequence: Problem and core design insight.
Contribution at system or algorithm level.
Principal evidence with evaluation scope.
Trade-off or limitation that affects interpretation.
Specific next question or bounded implication.
templates.when: The main contribution is an empirically evaluated method or system.

templates.name: Theory or resource closure
sequence: Formal or measurement gap addressed.
Main result or resource contribution.
What the result enables or reveals under stated assumptions.
Boundary of validity or coverage.
Concrete follow-up enabled by the contribution.
templates.when: The main contribution is a theorem, benchmark, dataset, or analysis.

guides.use_when: Drafting or revising the final paper section after claims, results, and limitations are stable.
verification: Every conclusion claim appears earlier with supporting evidence or analysis.
Numbers, comparisons, and scope match the final Results and Limitations sections.
No state-of-the-art, generalization, deployment, or causal claim is strengthened during summarization.
The final sentence communicates a specific implication or boundary rather than generic future work.

avoid: Thanking the reviewer without answering the question.
Claiming that the reviewer misunderstood when the manuscript omitted the needed distinction.
Promising broad experiments without completed results, resources, or permission.
Using significance, fairness, or state-of-the-art language without the required evidence.
inputs: The reviewer's concern decomposed into factual questions or requested actions.
Existing manuscript evidence, table or figure locations, analyses, and exact results available before the response deadline.
The valid scope of the current claim and any aspect that should be conceded.
Specific text, figure, table, appendix, or experiment changes that are actually authorized and feasible.
guides.label: Rebuttal: answer–evidence–revision with fixed evidence

checks: Separate misunderstanding, missing explanation, valid limitation, factual error, and request for new evidence.
Answer each atomic concern once and preserve the reviewer's strongest interpretation.
Do not frame disagreement as reviewer confusion when the manuscript was ambiguous.
moves.label: Classify the concern

checks: Begin with yes, no, agreement, correction, or a one-sentence scoped answer.
State the claim boundary before explanatory background when scope is disputed.
Acknowledge a valid concern without conceding unrelated claims.
moves.label: Lead with the answer

checks: Give the exact table, figure, equation, appendix, or result and state what it supports.
Report metric, denominator, comparison, runs, and uncertainty when the response relies on a number.
If evidence is absent, say so and narrow the claim instead of inventing a result.
moves.label: Point to existing evidence

checks: Describe the exact manuscript change and where it will appear.
Distinguish completed analysis from a promised revision or future experiment.
Ensure the revision resolves the stated concern rather than only adding volume.
moves.label: Commit to a concrete revision

guides.purpose: Respond directly to reviewer concerns using existing evidence, precise scope, and concrete manuscript changes while distinguishing correction, clarification, concession, and new work.

templates.name: Clarification with existing evidence
sequence: Direct scoped answer.
Exact existing evidence and what it establishes.
Source of ambiguity in the current manuscript.
Concrete clarification and location.
templates.when: The concern is addressed by evidence already in the submission but presentation is unclear.

templates.name: Valid limitation or missing evidence
sequence: Explicit agreement on the valid concern.
What the current evidence does and does not establish.
Narrowed claim or limitation statement.
Feasible revision, with new experiments labeled only if actually run.
templates.when: The reviewer identifies an unsupported scope, untested condition, or real weakness.

guides.use_when: Drafting a conference rebuttal, response-to-reviewers document, or concise answer to a technical concern.
verification: Every response begins with an answer rather than gratitude or background.
Every numeric or comparative statement matches the submission or a clearly identified completed addition.
Promises correspond to concrete edits that can be delivered under the venue rules.
Tone is factual and respectful without exaggerating agreement or certainty.
No citation, experiment, result, or venue policy is invented.

avoid: Translating words in source order before identifying the proposition.
Replacing technical terms with stylistically varied near-synonyms.
Strengthening may, can, suggests, or is associated with into proves or demonstrates.
Adding an explanatory clause that is plausible but absent from the source.
inputs: Source text plus its section, domain, intended readers, and neighboring sentences.
A terminology lock for method names, benchmark names, symbols, metrics, and repeated concepts.
The proposition structure: actor, action or relation, object, condition, comparison, evidence, negation, and modality.
Any primary source that must be checked for a technical definition or literature claim.
guides.label: Translation: proposition-first scientific English

checks: Identify who or what performs each action and what condition limits the statement.
Preserve negation, causal direction, quantifiers, uncertainty, comparison direction, and temporal order.
Resolve omitted Chinese subjects only from context; surface ambiguity instead of guessing.
moves.label: Recover the scientific proposition

checks: Retrieve the canonical term by domain without relying on literal dictionary equivalence.
Use one English form for each concept unless a distinction is intended.
Preserve symbols, method names, citation keys, metric units, dataset names, and capitalization.
moves.label: Lock technical terminology

checks: Choose sentence structure for the section and intent rather than mirroring Chinese word order.
Use attested collocations only when they match the proposition and rewrite original patterns around the facts.
Make comparison axes and antecedents explicit where English readers would otherwise misread them.
moves.label: Realize the section-specific discourse move

checks: Compare the translation against the source for omissions, additions, stronger modality, and reversed relations.
Check all numbers, units, parentheses, citations, equations, and respectively mappings.
Do not add explanations, praise, novelty, or evidence absent from the source.
moves.label: Back-check fidelity

guides.purpose: Translate Chinese AI-paper prose by preserving the scientific proposition, terminology, notation, evidence strength, and discourse function before realizing it in field-standard English.

templates.name: Technical proposition
sequence: Recover proposition and condition.
Lock terms and notation.
Select section-appropriate subject and verb.
Realize modifiers near the quantity or noun they constrain.
Back-check evidence strength and factual completeness.
templates.when: Translating method, experiment, or analysis prose.

templates.name: Definition or literature claim
sequence: Identify the exact definitional or literature proposition.
Verify the primary source and canonical term.
Paraphrase rather than present source-derived wording as a quotation.
Preserve citation scope and distinguish synthesis from source claims.
templates.when: The source defines a concept or characterizes prior work.

guides.use_when: Translating or bilingual-editing AI-paper text, captions, rebuttals, definitions, or technical explanations from Chinese into English.
verification: Back-translation preserves the same technical proposition, negation, comparison, and uncertainty.
Terminology is consistent with the paper and the target research community.
Every number, unit, symbol, citation, benchmark, and method name is unchanged unless correction was explicitly requested.
English syntax is natural for the target section and does not retain avoidable Chinese topic-comment structure.
No factual content, novelty claim, causal claim, or citation was added.
